In short: the lower layers (storage, permission, the pure deciders, the document engines) are well shaped. Above them, three oversized crates (vak-core, vak-agent, vak-server) hold the turn and nearly every feature, and that is where most of the work and most of the risk sit.

Built-in tools found: agent_network, ask_parent, automations, bash, commitments, doc_read, edit, flow, forget_memory, glob, grep, mail_calendar, office_apply, plan, propose_skill, read, recall, remember, skill, task, webfetch, workers, write.

Dependencies that point up

  • vak-catalog (L1) uses vak-llm
  • vak-config (L1) uses vak-control, vak-llm
  • vak-delivery (L2) uses vak-intent
  • vak-session (L1) uses vak-control, vak-intent, vak-llm

Each of these ties a lower layer to a higher one. When the data substrate imports model or intent types, a change to those types becomes a change to stored data, and the data contract only lets stored data grow.

The top is inverted as well. vak-core uses 25 crates, including the agent loop, so there is no small core a program could link against without pulling in nearly everything.

Sheet 03

Process topology

What runs at once on an installed machine. Drawn by hand.
long-lived processshort-lived child process, sandboxedshares fate: one process

Tools are isolated well: every built-in tool call, parser and MCP server crosses into a sandboxed child process. Everything else shares one process: the HTTP surface, the gateway, every live agent loop, provider streaming, schedulers and the storage code. The no-panic rule covers crashes, but nothing contains a slow leak, a blocking call on the async runtime, or a stuck lock. Any of those stalls every session and every channel together.

Sheet 04

One turn, end to end

Traced through the code. Drawn by hand; the names it uses are checked on every run.
  1. client → server
    The client posts a message. The server checks the bearer token, or the cookie plus a recognised Origin, then finds the live session handle and the workspace's Core in the pool.
  2. server → core
    Core::run_turn_with_message receives the session, the message, a cancel token, an approver, a permission engine, steering queues and an event channel.
  3. core
    run_turn_recorded, 1,647 lines in one function: it refuses an inactive, over-quota or standing-by Agent, takes a permission lease, resolves the route afresh, reads the capability epoch, resolves prompt layers, runs the intent resolver, picks commitments and builds the tool surface.
  4. core → ledger
    It mints the turn id and the RunId with its trace key and opens the run before anything else is written.
  5. core → agent
    The agent loop starts: run_message_inner, 1,848 lines in one function.
  6. agent → context
    plan_for_session picks the working set: the open turn word for word, plus the previous turn's card and nothing older. Assembly builds a stable prefix and a per-turn tail.
  7. llm
    complete_with_reliability walks the turn's route ladder with retries, Retry-After and the circuit breaker, and streams deltas with snapshots.
  8. agent → ledger
    Tool calls are read and normalised before the assistant message is written (read_arguments, then fill_defaults).
  9. agent
    authorize checks each call against the declared-reach permission engine and the provenance gate, and asks the approver when the answer is Ask.
  10. agent → worker
    Calls run in resource-claim waves. File and shell tools go to a sandboxed worker process. Card calls (show_card), recall, plan and task are handled inside the loop itself.
  11. worker → ledger
    Results, presentations and effects are written to the ledger. Large payloads go to the object store.
  12. agent
    Steps repeat until the model stops. Then the plan check compares the plan with receipts, and one correction goes through the ladder if something is missing.
  13. agent → ledger
    The turn card, decisions and work receipt are written, and Core settles the run.
  14. agent → server
    Agent events carry both a delta and a snapshot.
  15. server → client
    client_events::project sends what a person may see over SSE with sequence numbers, and the client draws each card by its form.

The sequence is sound and the record is thorough. Steps 3 and 5 to 12 are the two most complex functions in the system by clippy's measure, and most behaviour changes go through them; finding F1 has the evidence.

How state is kept

The substrate is a small database written by hand: encrypted content-addressed objects, per-entry sealed record frames in a hash chain, CAS refs with generations and writer epochs in SQLite, segments sealed by copy-verify-swap, Documents as versioned objects, rollups as projections, and a catalog tailer with one cursor per source.

Owning this layer, with no third-party database beyond the embedded SQLite for refs and the catalog, is a recorded decision. Its design is careful, and its size is the cost: 68 registered durable paths, each chain with its own reader, fencing on every write path, and erasure by destroying keys. The 2026-10-18 review found two P1 faults exactly in this layer:

A01: a cached grant kept authorizing after its revocation sat in an unreadable segment. A02: the global writer-epoch check and the ref update were not one transaction, so a fenced writer could still move a ref. See docs/plans/open-items.md for where their fixes stand.

One naming trap: the registry entry .env is the encrypted-file fallback for the Shared secret scope. The contract forbids literal .env files, so the name invites the wrong reading.

The work concentrates where the architecture is weakest. The three facade crates took most of the commits, while the well-shaped lower crates (permission, storage, ooxml, pdf, lifecycle) were written once and changed little.

Low churn in the lower crates is a good sign: they have clear contracts. High churn in the top three is the opposite. Every new behaviour lands in the same few files, because the boundaries that would let it land elsewhere don't exist.

Docs were touched in 56% of commits. Keeping the record true is a stated rule and it is followed, but each rule added to AGENTS.md (19,967 words) is enforced by whoever reads it, not by the type system or a crate boundary. The contract stands in for structure the code doesn't have.

Critic's findings

Only findings with a cost today. Each gives its evidence, why it matters and the fix. Numbers are live; the judgements were last reviewed at 8.9.0. Method: docs/architecture/review-method.md.
Structure shape of the codeLayering boundariesDrift the code disagrees with its own contractCaused a defect or confirmedContributes to defects elsewhere
F1
StructureCaused defects

Every turn runs through two outlier functions, and checks inside them interfere

Evidence. Clippy's cognitive_complexity scores Agent::run_message_inner at 194 (rank 1 of 4,348 library functions) and Core::run_turn_recorded at 103 (rank 3). The median function scores 3 and the 99th percentile 24. Following their current lines back with git log -L, 147 commits changed the first (6% of all commits) and 205 the second (9%). Fix commits land in vak-core/src/lib.rs at 10.2 and vak-agent/src/lib.rs at 9.3 per thousand lines, against a median of 4.5 over 396 files; file size alone does not predict the rate (ρ = -0.14).

Why it matters. Turn-scoped mutable state is shared across dozens of early exits, so checks interfere through it. In 797ae3b31 the /until-done hold's correction, the live stream's draft discard and the next step's repair framing collided, and the model apologised for an error it had not made. In d5420a83f the hold and the stop rules together let a model write filler to the step limit.

Fix. Make the turn's state one type, and run the end-of-turn checks as one ordered list through vak-control's ladder, with tests of how they combine. Context planning and the model call rarely cause bugs and can stay as they are.

Sheet 07; clippy at threshold 1, measured at 825b18564; evidence.py hotspots.

F2
StructureCaused a defect

A wrapping tool that misses one of the Tool trait's defaults fails silently

Evidence. Tool has 34 methods, 30 with a default body, and 29 implementations that override a median of 8. 2 wrappers must forward every declaration by hand, and one that forgets compiles cleanly and answers with the default:

  • ScopedWriteTool (crates/vak-agent/src/write_lease.rs:142): does not forward card_block, card_kinds, changes_workspace, presents_cards
  • BrokeredTool (crates/vak-tools/src/broker.rs:349): does not forward card_block, card_kinds, presents_cards

Why it matters. It has happened. fill_defaults joined the trait on 2026-10-07 (fb981ed3d), and both wrappers began forwarding it only on 2026-10-12 (53dbc16f8), so for five days every brokered tool lost its argument aliases. The gaps listed above answer correctly today only because no wrapped tool overrides those methods.

Fix. A test that fails when a wrapper leaves a defaulted method unforwarded, or a delegation macro that forwards them all.

crates/vak-tools/src/lib.rs (pub trait Tool); git log -S per method; evidence.py tool_wrappers.

F3
StructureContributes to F1's defects

Five separate vocabularies judge whether work is done

Evidence. 5 enums each describe whether work is finished, with 3, 9, 4, 5, 7 states, and production code translates between them in 3 places.

Why it matters. One piece of work can be judged five ways and nothing makes the answers agree. The interaction bugs in F1 sit where two of them meet: the commitment's /until-done hold and the stop rules.

Fix. One completion type the others project from, so a turn, a goal, managed work and a commitment cannot disagree about the same work.

F4
LayeringNo incident yet

The ledger stores the provider crate's message type

Evidence. vak-session names vak_llm:: 51 times, vak_intent:: 31 times and vak_control:: 20 times. The stored message is vak_llm::ContentBlock, including an opaque Provider variant that carries a provider's own payload. Of 19 commits to vak-llm/src/types.rs, 7 also changed vak-session, and a change to vak-llm rebuilds 20 crates.

Why it matters. Invariant 1 needs every request rebuilt exactly from the ledger, and storing the wire type is the direct way to get that. But under the additive-only data contract every wire type becomes a stored format that can never change, and a provider's opaque payload is stored data no reader in Vak understands.

Fix. A message type the ledger owns, converted at the provider boundary, keeps invariant 1 and frees the wire types.

crates/vak-session/src; crates/vak-llm/src/types.rs history; evidence.py ledger_types and fanout.

F5
StructureDefects found by review

The riskiest boundaries are tested least for the faults that hit them

Evidence. Storage has torn-write, crash, fsync and fault-injection tests and a fuzz corpus, but no model-based tests of a chain's reader and few tests with two writer processes. The two P1 faults of 2026-10-18 needed exactly those shapes: an unreadable segment between a grant and its revocation (A01), and a writer paused between two checks (A02). A review found them, not the suite. Elsewhere, counting every #[test] per thousand source lines (median 12.0): vak-catalog, which decides who may see each search result, has 3.3; vak-pdf, which parses hostile files, has 4.0 and no fuzz targets.

Sheet 10

What to keep, and a sound shape

Well-shaped parts worth keeping as they are

vak-permission1,166 lines, declared reach, universal Allow, an adversarial escape corpus. Small and central.
vak-control · vak-judge · vak-lifecyclePure deciders with no vak dependencies. The right shape for policy.
vak-context3,276 lines of pure planning and assembly over the ledger.
vak-ooxml · vak-pdfNo vak dependencies, bounded, fuzzable, run only in the worker.
Worker boundaryA versioned protocol with 14 task kinds; parsers and tools never run in the server process.
Effects, runs, cursorsAt-most-once outbound actions and unknown outcomes that are never re-sent automatically. Rare and correct.
Provenance gatePrivate data plus someone else's words means a human approves anything that leaves the machine.
vak-llm capability declarationsWire features declared by the adapter and learned from refusal, never inferred from a provider's name.

A shape that would hold

The test for this shape: someone outside the project writes an agent in Python against the kernel API in an afternoon, gets sandboxing, effects, provenance and audit without reading AGENTS.md, and it still works after the next release. The parts that would make that possible are already written. They sit under vak-core, vak-agent and vak-server rather than being exposed.

How this is measured: source lines from src/**/*.rs (inline unit tests included), test lines from tests/**, dependencies from cargo metadata --no-deps, commits from git log -- <path> (commits that touch only this page are left out), function lengths from header to closing brace.
